WarMonitor RT @gtconway3d : “We are now entirely dependent on software systems that almost nobody understands end to end, that increasingly few people can repair, and that attackers can now probe at machine speed. … “We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability.” I haven’t lived here in awhile, but I see no other way to answer the hundreds of texts/DMs asking me if the world is, indeed, ending. In the span of six days, we’ve experienced; 11/12 — Microsoft outage 11/13 — Nationwide FAA ground stop 11/16 — Major US banking disruptions 11/17 — NSA’s classified internal network goes down We need far more analysis of why so much is breaking at once. I don’t want to get out over my skis here, and what I am hearing does not contradict the messaging that most of this is the result of screwy updates. But stepping back, the dots are starting to form a collective picture. We are seeing: • An explosion in severe and critical vulnerabilities, with AI accelerating discovery to 3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year. This is collectively being referred to as “vulnageddon” or “the vulnpocalypse.” • Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS. AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them. • Powerful AI-enabled offensive tools like ARTEX have been thrown into the hands of every third tier nation state, cybercriminal and digital arsonist, which logically creates havoc. • This creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates, increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways. • Pressure to just “AI everything” means we are rolling out automated AI tooling on top of brittle infrastructure that can’t support it. My generation grew up in an extraordinary period of technological stability. We worked our way up the software stack, abstracting away layer after layer, until we lost a fundamental understanding of how the underlying systems actually work. We were told to “move fast and break things.” VCS told us to celebrate the idea that “software would eat the world.” Now we’re telling ourselves we can simply “roll out AI” across everything, as though nothing underneath will buckle. We never stopped to ask: SHOULD WE? Should we be digitizing every last nook and cranny of our companies, infrastructure, healthcare, homes, cars, bodies, lives? Especially when the complexity, interdependence, and fragility we were introducing overwhelmed our ability to understand/secure/maintain the systems we built? Nobody every asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history? We are now entirely dependent on software systems that almost nobody understands end to end, that increasingly few people can repair, and that attackers can now probe at machine speed. Open Source Intel The Islamic regime says it would never use a dirty bomb. Last month, a Tehran University professor openly discussed dirty bombs as a way for Iran to deter US and Israel. Hamza Safavi, the son of a former IRGC commander, discussed unconventional weapons in interviews in August and October. “I believe that in order to reach this concept meaning deterrence we don’t necessarily need the atomic bomb,” Safavi said. “Conversely, Iran can render Israel uninhabitable using both conventional and unconventional weapons in its arsenal.” Asked what he meant by unconventional weapons, he replied, “Yes, dirty bombs, chemical weapons, and other examples.” Safavi also questioned whether Iran had disclosed its full stockpile of enriched uranium. “As I have noted elsewhere, there’s an ambiguity as to whether Iran’s total enriched uranium stockpile is limited to 400 kilograms. And I really like this ambiguity.” “Who can guarantee that the declared uranium is all we have?” On Israel, Safavi said, “If the game becomes dirty, Iran has the necessary countermeasures.” “If we are not going to survive, Israel will not survive either.” In June, Iranian economist Muhammad Resa Yazad claimed that dirty bombs could “render the target city uninhabitable due to the level of contamination.” He also threatened retaliation against the U.S. “If we are hit, we will attack Washington. They know we have the missile range to do this.” tweet

Nuno Felix RT @specialopsmag : Pitted against thousands of US Army paratroopers, tracking dogs, and thermal imaging drones, Polish Special Forces have become the first NATO ally to complete Exercise Deep Strike. The operators successfully infiltrated enemy lines, covered nearly 100 km undetected through forests and farmlands, and delivered a simulated drone strike on a target. The exercise, designed by US Special Operations Command Europe and shaped by lessons from Ukraine, was held in late August in Germany. Operating light and deliberately low-tech, relying on map and compass navigation, and thermal camouflage instead of GPS or advanced electronics, the operators slipped through the lines, marched for days, and struck a simulated electronic warfare asset with an attack drone carrying a dummy charge. Strong work by Poland’s special forces and a clear signal of Allied readiness. tweet

Matan Kahana elected as Israel's Knesset speaker as opposition seeks to replace Netanyahu Israel’s Knesset has elected Matan Kahana, a member of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, as its speaker, in a vote seen as a boost for the opposition leader’s efforts to replace Benjamin Netanyahu. Kahana secured 66 votes, compared with 52 for Netanyahu’s nominee, with support from Palestinian members of the Knesset proving significant. The result strengthens Eisenkot’s influence over the legislative agenda, but forming a governing coalition remains complicated by divisions within the opposition, particularly over whether to rely on support from Palestinian-Israeli parties. Eisenkot is also holding talks with ultra-Orthodox parties, whose possible abstention could help him secure a parliamentary majority. @Al Jazeera English | Subscribe
